points.area: Key science skills
points.title: Aims, hypotheses and variables
points.detail: Writing a research question and testable hypothesis, and identifying independent, dependent and controlled variables in environmental investigations.

questions.q: A student investigates the effect of distance from a road on lichen cover. Write a hypothesis and identify the variables.
answer: Hypothesis: as distance from the road increases, the percentage cover of lichen on tree trunks will increase.
Independent variable: distance from the road, measured in metres.
Dependent variable: percentage cover of lichen, measured using a quadrat.
Controlled variables include tree species, trunk aspect, height above ground and time of sampling.

card.title: Aims, hypotheses and variables
back: Writing a research question and testable hypothesis, and identifying independent, dependent and controlled variables in environmental investigations.

points.area: Key science skills
points.title: Sampling in the field
points.detail: Quadrats, transects, random and systematic sampling, sample size and the sources of bias in environmental fieldwork.

questions.q: Explain the difference between random and systematic sampling and when each is appropriate.
answer: Random sampling places quadrats at coordinates chosen by chance, which avoids observer bias and suits a relatively uniform area.
Systematic sampling places them at fixed intervals, usually along a transect, which suits an area with an environmental gradient.
Systematic sampling is used to detect how a variable changes with distance, such as from a shoreline or pollution source.
Sample size matters in both, since too few quadrats produce results dominated by local variation rather than the pattern being investigated.

card.title: Sampling in the field
back: Quadrats, transects, random and systematic sampling, sample size and the sources of bias in environmental fieldwork.

points.area: Key science skills
points.title: Accuracy, precision and validity
points.detail: Distinguishing these terms, identifying random and systematic error in field measurement, and evaluating environmental data.

questions.q: A water quality meter consistently reads 0.4 pH units higher than a calibration standard. Classify the error and state the remedy.
answer: This is a systematic error, since every reading is displaced in the same direction by a similar amount.
The results may be precise but they are not accurate, because they are consistently offset from the true value.
The remedy is to recalibrate the meter against known standards before use, and to recheck calibration during long sampling sessions.

card.title: Accuracy, precision and validity
back: Distinguishing these terms, identifying random and systematic error in field measurement, and evaluating environmental data.

points.area: Key science skills
points.title: Ethics and fieldwork responsibility
points.detail: Minimising disturbance, permits for protected areas and species, respect for Traditional Owners and safe working practices in the field.

questions.q: Explain three responsibilities a student has when conducting environmental fieldwork.
answer: Minimise disturbance: avoid trampling vegetation, return moved objects and animals, and take only the samples required.
Obtain permission: access to private land, reserves and protected species usually requires permits and landholder consent, and engagement with Traditional Owners where relevant.
Work safely: complete a risk assessment covering terrain, weather, water and wildlife, and never conduct fieldwork alone.

card.title: Ethics and fieldwork responsibility
back: Minimising disturbance, permits for protected areas and species, respect for Traditional Owners and safe working practices in the field.

points.area: Unit 3: How can biodiversity and development be sustained? — AoS 1: Why is maintaining biodiversity worth a sustained effort?
points.title: Levels of biodiversity
points.detail: Genetic, species and ecosystem diversity, how each is measured and why each matters for resilience.

questions.q: Name the three levels of biodiversity and explain why genetic diversity matters for a population's survival.
answer: The three levels are genetic diversity within a species, species diversity within an ecosystem and ecosystem diversity across a region.
Genetic diversity is the variation in alleles present within a population.
A population with high genetic diversity is more likely to contain individuals with alleles suited to new conditions such as disease or climate change.
A population with low diversity has less raw material for natural selection, so it is far more vulnerable to being eliminated by a single pressure.

card.title: Levels of biodiversity
back: Genetic, species and ecosystem diversity, how each is measured and why each matters for resilience.

points.area: Unit 3: How can biodiversity and development be sustained? — AoS 1: Why is maintaining biodiversity worth a sustained effort?
points.title: Ecosystem services
points.detail: Provisioning, regulating, supporting and cultural services, and the difficulty of valuing them in economic decisions.

questions.q: Name the four categories of ecosystem service with an example of each, and explain why they are often undervalued.
answer: Provisioning services supply tangible goods such as food, timber, fresh water and medicines.
Regulating services include climate regulation, pollination, water purification and flood control.
Supporting services such as soil formation and nutrient cycling underpin all the others, and cultural services include recreation and spiritual value.
They are undervalued because most are not traded in markets and have no price, so decisions based on financial cost alone treat them as free.

card.title: Ecosystem services
back: Provisioning, regulating, supporting and cultural services, and the difficulty of valuing them in economic decisions.

points.area: Unit 3: How can biodiversity and development be sustained? — AoS 1: Why is maintaining biodiversity worth a sustained effort?
points.title: Threats to biodiversity
points.detail: Habitat loss and fragmentation, invasive species, overexploitation, pollution and climate change, and their interaction.

questions.q: Explain how habitat fragmentation threatens biodiversity beyond the direct loss of area.
answer: Fragmentation divides continuous habitat into isolated patches separated by cleared or developed land.
Small patches support smaller populations, which are more vulnerable to genetic drift, inbreeding and local extinction.
Isolation prevents movement between patches, so recolonisation after a local loss becomes unlikely and gene flow is restricted.
Increased edge relative to interior alters microclimate, light and wind and allows predators and weeds to penetrate, degrading the remaining habitat.

card.title: Threats to biodiversity
back: Habitat loss and fragmentation, invasive species, overexploitation, pollution and climate change, and their interaction.

points.area: Unit 3: How can biodiversity and development be sustained? — AoS 1: Why is maintaining biodiversity worth a sustained effort?
points.title: Invasive species
points.detail: The characteristics of successful invaders, their ecological and economic impacts, and management approaches.

questions.q: Explain why introduced species can become invasive and describe two management approaches.
answer: An introduced species often arrives without the predators, parasites and competitors that limited it in its native range.
If it also reproduces rapidly, disperses widely and tolerates a range of conditions, its population can expand without natural control.
Prevention through biosecurity and border inspection is the most cost-effective approach, since eradication after establishment is far harder.
Control methods include physical removal, targeted baiting and biological control, though biological control requires extensive testing to ensure the agent does not attack native species.

card.title: Invasive species
back: The characteristics of successful invaders, their ecological and economic impacts, and management approaches.

points.area: Unit 3: How can biodiversity and development be sustained? — AoS 1: Why is maintaining biodiversity worth a sustained effort?
points.title: Conservation strategies
points.detail: Protected areas, wildlife corridors, captive breeding, revegetation, and the comparison of in situ and ex situ conservation.

questions.q: Compare in situ and ex situ conservation, giving an advantage and a limitation of each.
answer: In situ conservation protects species within their natural habitat, through reserves, corridors and habitat restoration.
Its advantage is that it conserves the whole ecosystem and allows natural selection and ecological relationships to continue.
Ex situ conservation maintains species outside their habitat, in zoos, botanic gardens or seed banks.

Its advantage is protecting species whose habitat is too degraded to sustain them, but populations are small, adaptation to captivity can occur, and reintroduction often fails without habitat restoration.

card.title: Conservation strategies
back: Protected areas, wildlife corridors, captive breeding, revegetation, and the comparison of in situ and ex situ conservation.

points.area: Unit 3: How can biodiversity and development be sustained? — AoS 1: Why is maintaining biodiversity worth a sustained effort?
points.title: Indigenous land management
points.detail: The role of Traditional Owner knowledge and practice, including cultural burning, in maintaining ecosystems and biodiversity.

questions.q: Explain how cultural burning differs from hazard reduction burning and its ecological benefits.
answer: Cultural burning uses frequent, low-intensity, small-scale fires timed according to detailed knowledge of season, weather and the condition of particular Country.
It is applied selectively rather than as broad-area treatment, and is guided by the requirements of specific plants and animals.
Ecologically it maintains a mosaic of vegetation at different stages, which supports species with different habitat requirements.
It also reduces fuel loads gradually, lowering the risk of high-intensity fire that destroys canopy, soil structure and seed banks.

card.title: Indigenous land management
back: The role of Traditional Owner knowledge and practice, including cultural burning, in maintaining ecosystems and biodiversity.

points.area: Unit 3: How can biodiversity and development be sustained? — AoS 1: Why is maintaining biodiversity worth a sustained effort?
points.title: Monitoring and indicator species
points.detail: The use of indicator species, ecological surveys and long-term monitoring to detect environmental change.

questions.q: Explain what makes a species a useful environmental indicator and give an example.
answer: A useful indicator is sensitive to the environmental change of interest, responding measurably before the wider ecosystem is affected.
It should be well studied, easily identified and sampled, and widely distributed so comparisons can be made across sites.
Aquatic macroinvertebrates are used to indicate water quality, since particular groups tolerate very different levels of pollution and oxygen.
The composition of the community therefore reflects conditions over time, rather than the single moment that a chemical test measures.

card.title: Monitoring and indicator species
back: The use of indicator species, ecological surveys and long-term monitoring to detect environmental change.

points.area: Unit 3: How can biodiversity and development be sustained? — AoS 2: When is development sustainable?
points.title: Dimensions and principles of sustainability
points.detail: Ecological, economic and sociocultural dimensions of sustainable development and the principles used to judge environmental management.

questions.q: Explain how the three dimensions of sustainability and two sustainability principles could be applied to an environmental development.
answer: Identify the ecological, economic and sociocultural dimensions and show that a sustainable decision considers all three.
Apply two relevant principles, such as intergenerational equity, conservation of biodiversity, efficient resource use, precaution or user pays.
Link each principle to a concrete feature or likely impact of the development.
Reach a supported judgement about whether the proposal is sustainable.

card.title: Dimensions and principles of sustainability
back: Ecological, economic and sociocultural dimensions of sustainable development and the principles used to judge environmental management.

points.area: Unit 3: How can biodiversity and development be sustained? — AoS 2: When is development sustainable?
points.title: Earth systems and environmental impacts
points.detail: Using interactions among the atmosphere, biosphere, hydrosphere and lithosphere to analyse beneficial and harmful impacts.

questions.q: Analyse two ways a development could create impacts across more than one Earth system.
answer: Identify the affected Earth systems.
Explain the process linking an action in one system to a change in another.
Include at least one beneficial or harmful impact supported by evidence.
Recognise that feedbacks and indirect effects can extend beyond the development site.

card.title: Earth systems and environmental impacts
back: Using interactions among the atmosphere, biosphere, hydrosphere and lithosphere to analyse beneficial and harmful impacts.

points.area: Unit 3: How can biodiversity and development be sustained? — AoS 2: When is development sustainable?
points.title: Stakeholders and environmental decision-making
points.detail: How stakeholder values, knowledge and priorities create interconnections and tensions in responsible environmental decisions.

questions.q: Explain why two stakeholders may reach different conclusions about the same environmental proposal.
answer: Identify the stakeholders and their relevant values, knowledge or priorities.
Explain how those differences affect the evidence or impacts each prioritises.
Describe a genuine tension or trade-off between their positions.
Connect the disagreement to the eventual environmental-management decision.

card.title: Stakeholders and environmental decision-making
back: How stakeholder values, knowledge and priorities create interconnections and tensions in responsible environmental decisions.

points.area: Unit 3: How can biodiversity and development be sustained? — AoS 2: When is development sustainable?
points.title: Risk and cost-benefit analysis
points.detail: Qualitative risk analysis and cost-benefit analysis as tools for integrated sustainability assessment.

questions.q: Apply qualitative risk analysis and cost-benefit analysis to an environmental management option.
answer: For risk, consider likelihood and consequence rather than consequence alone.
For cost-benefit analysis, compare relevant environmental, economic and sociocultural costs and benefits.
Explain uncertainty or limitations in the available evidence.
Use both tools to justify a recommendation.

card.title: Risk and cost-benefit analysis
back: Qualitative risk analysis and cost-benefit analysis as tools for integrated sustainability assessment.

points.area: Unit 3: How can biodiversity and development be sustained? — AoS 2: When is development sustainable?
points.title: Circular economy and resource efficiency
points.detail: Circular-economy thinking, resource efficiency and the challenge of reducing waste while maintaining useful services.

questions.q: Explain how circular-economy thinking could improve the sustainability of a selected development.
answer: Replace the linear take-make-dispose model with strategies that retain materials and value.
Apply reuse, repair, remanufacture, recycling or design-out-waste to the case.
Explain an environmental benefit and a possible economic or social trade-off.
Relate the strategy to efficient resource use or another sustainability principle.

card.title: Circular economy and resource efficiency
back: Circular-economy thinking, resource efficiency and the challenge of reducing waste while maintaining useful services.

points.area: Unit 3: How can biodiversity and development be sustained? — AoS 2: When is development sustainable?
points.title: Evaluating an environmental management strategy
points.detail: Using aims, monitoring data, regulation, technology and sustainability principles to evaluate the effectiveness of a case-study strategy.

questions.q: Evaluate the effectiveness of an environmental management strategy used in a case study.
answer: State the strategy’s aim and the criteria used to judge it.
Use relevant monitoring data or other evidence to assess outcomes.
Consider implementation, regulation, stakeholder response, technology and unintended impacts.
Reach a balanced judgement linked to sustainability principles.

card.title: Evaluating an environmental management strategy
back: Using aims, monitoring data, regulation, technology and sustainability principles to evaluate the effectiveness of a case-study strategy.

points.area: Unit 4: How can climate change and the impacts of human energy use be managed? — AoS 1: How can we respond to climate change?
points.title: The greenhouse effect
points.detail: The natural greenhouse effect, the enhanced greenhouse effect, the major greenhouse gases and their relative warming potentials.

questions.q: Explain the difference between the natural and the enhanced greenhouse effect.
answer: Solar radiation passes through the atmosphere and warms the surface, which re-emits energy as longer wavelength infrared radiation.
Greenhouse gases absorb some of this outgoing infrared radiation and re-emit it in all directions, warming the lower atmosphere.
This natural effect keeps the earth roughly 33 degrees warmer than it would otherwise be and makes life possible.
The enhanced effect is the additional warming caused by human emissions raising greenhouse gas concentrations, which traps more outgoing radiation and raises average temperatures.

card.title: The greenhouse effect
back: The natural greenhouse effect, the enhanced greenhouse effect, the major greenhouse gases and their relative warming potentials.

points.area: Unit 4: How can climate change and the impacts of human energy use be managed? — AoS 1: How can we respond to climate change?
points.title: Evidence for climate change
points.detail: Instrumental records, ice cores, tree rings, sea level and ice extent data, and the convergence of independent lines of evidence.

questions.q: Describe three independent lines of evidence for recent climate change and explain why convergence matters.
answer: Instrumental temperature records from land stations, ships and satellites show rising global average temperature since the industrial era.
Ice cores provide past temperature and atmospheric composition, showing current carbon dioxide concentrations far above the range of recent hundreds of thousands of years.
Physical indicators including glacier retreat, declining sea ice extent, rising sea level and earlier spring events corroborate the temperature record.
Convergence matters because these methods have different assumptions and error sources, so agreement between them cannot be explained by a fault in any single method.

card.title: Evidence for climate change
back: Instrumental records, ice cores, tree rings, sea level and ice extent data, and the convergence of independent lines of evidence.

points.area: Unit 4: How can climate change and the impacts of human energy use be managed? — AoS 1: How can we respond to climate change?
points.title: Feedback mechanisms
points.detail: Positive feedbacks such as ice-albedo and permafrost methane release, negative feedbacks, and the concept of tipping points.

questions.q: Explain the ice-albedo feedback and why positive feedbacks make prediction difficult.
answer: Ice and snow have high albedo and reflect most incoming solar radiation back to space.
Warming melts ice, exposing darker ocean or land with much lower albedo, which absorbs more radiation and causes further warming.
This is a positive feedback because the output of the process amplifies the input that produced it.
Positive feedbacks complicate prediction because the response is not proportional to the forcing, and beyond a tipping point the change may continue without further human emissions.

card.title: Feedback mechanisms
back: Positive feedbacks such as ice-albedo and permafrost methane release, negative feedbacks, and the concept of tipping points.

points.area: Unit 4: How can climate change and the impacts of human energy use be managed? — AoS 1: How can we respond to climate change?
points.title: Impacts of climate change
points.detail: Effects on temperature extremes, rainfall, sea level, ocean acidification, ecosystems, agriculture and human settlement.

questions.q: Explain ocean acidification and its ecological consequences.
answer: The ocean absorbs a substantial proportion of atmospheric carbon dioxide, which reacts with water to form carbonic acid.
This lowers ocean pH and reduces the concentration of carbonate ions available in the water.
Organisms that build shells and skeletons from calcium carbonate, including corals, molluscs and some plankton, find it harder to form and maintain those structures.
Because many of these species are at the base of marine food webs or build reef habitat, the effects propagate through entire ecosystems.

card.title: Impacts of climate change
back: Effects on temperature extremes, rainfall, sea level, ocean acidification, ecosystems, agriculture and human settlement.

points.area: Unit 4: How can climate change and the impacts of human energy use be managed? — AoS 1: How can we respond to climate change?
points.title: Mitigation
points.detail: Reducing emissions at source, carbon sequestration, changes in energy, transport, industry and land use, and the role of policy.

questions.q: Distinguish mitigation from adaptation and give two examples of each.
answer: Mitigation reduces the magnitude of climate change by reducing greenhouse gas emissions or removing gases from the atmosphere.
Examples include replacing fossil generation with renewables, and reforestation to sequester carbon.
Adaptation reduces the harm from changes that are already occurring or now unavoidable.
Examples include building sea walls and drainage for higher sea levels, and shifting to drought-tolerant crop varieties; both are needed, since past emissions commit the climate to further change.

card.title: Mitigation
back: Reducing emissions at source, carbon sequestration, changes in energy, transport, industry and land use, and the role of policy.

points.area: Unit 4: How can climate change and the impacts of human energy use be managed? — AoS 1: How can we respond to climate change?
points.title: Responses and their evaluation
points.detail: International agreements, national targets, carbon pricing and offsets, and criteria for judging whether a response is effective.

questions.q: Explain how carbon pricing is intended to reduce emissions and two criticisms of it.
answer: Carbon pricing attaches a cost to emitting greenhouse gases, either through a tax or through a cap and trade market.
This internalises the external cost, making low-emission alternatives relatively cheaper and creating an incentive to abate wherever it is cheapest.
One criticism is that it is regressive, since energy costs consume a larger share of low income household budgets unless revenue is redistributed.
Another is that emissions may simply relocate to jurisdictions without a price, which is carbon leakage, so the global reduction is smaller than the national figures suggest.

card.title: Responses and their evaluation
back: International agreements, national targets, carbon pricing and offsets, and criteria for judging whether a response is effective.

points.area: Unit 4: How can climate change and the impacts of human energy use be managed? — AoS 2: What might be a more sustainable mix of energy sources?
points.title: Energy sources and classification
points.detail: Renewable and non-renewable sources, energy density, and the distinction between a primary energy source and an energy carrier.

questions.q: Distinguish between a renewable energy source and an energy carrier, and explain why hydrogen is a carrier.
answer: A renewable source is replenished on a human timescale, such as solar, wind, hydro and biomass.
An energy carrier stores and transports energy that was generated elsewhere, rather than being a source in its own right.
Hydrogen is a carrier because it must be produced using energy, usually from electrolysis or reforming natural gas.
Its environmental value therefore depends entirely on the energy used to produce it, which is why green and grey hydrogen are distinguished.

card.title: Energy sources and classification
back: Renewable and non-renewable sources, energy density, and the distinction between a primary energy source and an energy carrier.

points.area: Unit 4: How can climate change and the impacts of human energy use be managed? — AoS 2: What might be a more sustainable mix of energy sources?
points.title: Fossil fuels and their impacts
points.detail: Formation, combustion, emissions of carbon dioxide and other pollutants, and impacts across extraction, transport and use.

questions.q: Explain three environmental impacts of coal-fired electricity generation across its life cycle.
answer: Extraction disturbs land, destroys habitat and can contaminate groundwater and surface water with acid mine drainage.
Combustion releases carbon dioxide contributing to the enhanced greenhouse effect, plus sulfur and nitrogen oxides causing acid rain and particulates harming respiratory health.
Generation requires large volumes of cooling water and returns heated water, causing thermal pollution of waterways.
Ash and residues require long-term disposal, and heavy metals including mercury can enter food chains.

card.title: Fossil fuels and their impacts
back: Formation, combustion, emissions of carbon dioxide and other pollutants, and impacts across extraction, transport and use.

points.area: Unit 4: How can climate change and the impacts of human energy use be managed? — AoS 2: What might be a more sustainable mix of energy sources?
points.title: Solar and wind energy
points.detail: How each generates electricity, capacity factors, intermittency, land and material requirements, and their environmental trade-offs.

questions.q: Explain the problem of intermittency in solar and wind generation and two ways it is managed.
answer: Output depends on weather and time of day, so generation does not automatically match demand.
Storage manages this by capturing surplus generation in batteries or pumped hydro and releasing it when generation falls.
Interconnection across a wide geographic area also helps, since wind conditions differ between regions and averaging reduces variability.
Demand management and dispatchable backup generation complete the system, so intermittency is a system design problem rather than a barrier in itself.

card.title: Solar and wind energy
back: How each generates electricity, capacity factors, intermittency, land and material requirements, and their environmental trade-offs.

points.area: Unit 4: How can climate change and the impacts of human energy use be managed? — AoS 2: What might be a more sustainable mix of energy sources?
points.title: Hydro, geothermal and bioenergy
points.detail: The operation and environmental consequences of each, including river ecology, land use and the carbon balance of biomass.

questions.q: Explain why bioenergy is described as carbon neutral in principle, and why in practice it may not be.
answer: Biomass absorbs carbon dioxide as it grows, so combustion in principle returns carbon that was recently removed from the atmosphere.
In practice, energy is consumed in cultivation, fertiliser production, harvesting, processing and transport, usually from fossil sources.
If forest is cleared for fuel crops, the carbon stored in the original vegetation and soil is released and takes decades to recover.
Land used for fuel also competes with food production, so the net benefit depends heavily on the feedstock and how it is grown.

card.title: Hydro, geothermal and bioenergy
back: The operation and environmental consequences of each, including river ecology, land use and the carbon balance of biomass.

points.area: Unit 4: How can climate change and the impacts of human energy use be managed? — AoS 2: What might be a more sustainable mix of energy sources?
points.title: Nuclear energy
points.detail: Fission, the absence of operational carbon emissions, waste management, safety and the debate over its role in decarbonisation.

questions.q: Evaluate nuclear power as a low-carbon energy source, giving two advantages and two concerns.
answer: Advantages: generation produces almost no greenhouse gases, and output is continuous rather than weather dependent, providing reliable baseload capacity.
It also has a very high energy density, so fuel and land requirements per unit of electricity are small.
Concerns: high-level waste remains hazardous for thousands of years and requires secure long-term storage that few countries have established.
Construction costs and timeframes are very large, and although serious accidents are rare their consequences are severe and long lasting.

card.title: Nuclear energy
back: Fission, the absence of operational carbon emissions, waste management, safety and the debate over its role in decarbonisation.

points.area: Unit 4: How can climate change and the impacts of human energy use be managed? — AoS 2: What might be a more sustainable mix of energy sources?
points.title: Life cycle assessment of energy systems
points.detail: Comparing energy sources across construction, operation, decommissioning and disposal rather than at the point of generation alone.

questions.q: Explain why energy sources must be compared using life cycle assessment rather than operational emissions alone.
answer: Operational emissions capture only the generation stage, which favours technologies whose impacts occur during construction.
Manufacturing solar panels and wind turbines requires mining, refining and energy-intensive processing, which produces emissions before any electricity is generated.
Decommissioning and disposal impose further impacts, including waste from panels, blades and nuclear materials.
Only a whole-of-life comparison allows a fair judgement, and on that basis renewables and nuclear remain far lower than fossil fuels.

card.title: Life cycle assessment of energy systems
card.front: Life cycle assessment of energy systems
back: Comparing energy sources across construction, operation, decommissioning and disposal rather than at the point of generation alone.

points.area: Unit 4: How can climate change and the impacts of human energy use be managed? — AoS 2: What might be a more sustainable mix of energy sources?
points.title: Energy efficiency and demand management
points.detail: Reducing energy use through efficiency, behaviour and design, and the rebound effect that can offset savings.

questions.q: Explain the rebound effect and why efficiency alone may not reduce total energy consumption.
answer: Efficiency reduces the energy needed to deliver a service, which reduces its cost to the user.
Lower running costs encourage greater use, so some of the expected saving is consumed by increased consumption.
For example, a more efficient vehicle costs less per kilometre, which may lead to more driving.
Efficiency therefore needs to be combined with pricing, regulation or behaviour change if total consumption is to fall.

card.title: Energy efficiency and demand management
back: Reducing energy use through efficiency, behaviour and design, and the rebound effect that can offset savings.

points.area: Unit 4: How can climate change and the impacts of human energy use be managed? — AoS 3: How is scientific inquiry used to investigate contemporary environmental challenges?
points.title: Designing an environmental investigation
points.detail: Developing a question, selecting a methodology, planning field or laboratory work and identifying controls and limitations.

questions.q: Explain why controlling variables is harder in field investigations than in the laboratory, and how investigators respond.
answer: Field conditions such as weather, soil, aspect and species composition vary continuously and cannot be held constant.
Investigators therefore control what they can, such as sampling at the same time of day and using the same technique at every site.
They increase the number of replicates so random variation averages out rather than dominating the result.
They also record uncontrolled conditions, so these can be considered when interpreting results and acknowledged as limitations.

card.title: Designing an environmental investigation
back: Developing a question, selecting a methodology, planning field or laboratory work and identifying controls and limitations.

points.area: Unit 4: How can climate change and the impacts of human energy use be managed? — AoS 3: How is scientific inquiry used to investigate contemporary environmental challenges?
points.title: Processing and presenting environmental data
points.detail: Tabulating and graphing field data, calculating means and percentage cover, and choosing representations that show a pattern clearly.

questions.q: A student samples species richness at six distances along a transect. State the appropriate graph and justify the choice.
answer: A line graph or scatter plot with a line of best fit is appropriate, with distance on the horizontal axis.
Distance is a continuous independent variable, so intermediate values are meaningful and a connected or fitted line shows the trend.
The graph should show every replicate or include error bars, so the variability behind each mean is visible.

card.title: Processing and presenting environmental data
back: Tabulating and graphing field data, calculating means and percentage cover, and choosing representations that show a pattern clearly.

points.area: Unit 4: How can climate change and the impacts of human energy use be managed? — AoS 3: How is scientific inquiry used to investigate contemporary environmental challenges?
points.title: Analysing, evaluating and communicating
points.detail: Identifying trends, distinguishing correlation from causation, evaluating the method and communicating findings to an audience.

questions.q: A student finds lichen cover increases with distance from a road and concludes vehicle pollution kills lichen. Evaluate this conclusion.
answer: The data establish a correlation between distance and lichen cover, which is consistent with the hypothesis.
They do not establish causation, since the investigation did not manipulate pollution levels or exclude other variables.
Confounding factors could explain the pattern, including changes in light, humidity, tree age or disturbance with distance from the road.
The conclusion should state that the results are consistent with an effect of vehicle pollution, and identify what further evidence, such as direct air quality measurement, would be required.

card.title: Analysing, evaluating and communicating
back: Identifying trends, distinguishing correlation from causation, evaluating the method and communicating findings to an audience.
